hints: Notice that both salts first do the same simple acid-base reaction to make HX, so focus on what happens to the HX after it forms.
Look at the extra products with NaI: $\text{I}_2$, $\text{SO}_2$, $\text{S}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{S}$. Sulfur is being reduced while iodide is oxidised.
Compare the ability of $\text{Cl}^-$ and $\text{I}^-$ to give away electrons to concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ acting as an oxidising agent.
walkthrough:
**Spot the common first reaction**

Both solids first act as bases toward concentrated sulfuric acid. This is a simple proton transfer.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{NaX} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{NaHSO}_4 + \text{HX}$$
where $\text{X}$ is $\text{Cl}$ or $\text{I}$.

**Ask what the HX can do next**

Concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is a strong oxidising agent. Whether it is reduced further depends on how good a reducing agent the halide ion is.

Think of reducing power down Group 17: $\text{Cl}^- < \text{Br}^- < \text{I}^-$. Iodide loses electrons most easily.

**Explain the observed difference**

$\text{Cl}^-$ is too weak a reducing agent, so the reaction stops at $\text{HCl}$. $\text{I}^-$ is a strong enough reducing agent to reduce sulfur from +6 in $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to +4, 0 and -2.

Typical further reactions:
$$2\text{HI} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{I}_2 + \text{SO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
and further to $\text{S}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{S}$. That is why many extra products appear only with NaI.

options.A: Incorrect. Halogen displacement is $\text{Cl}_2$ displacing $\text{I}_2$ from $\text{I}^-$, not $\text{Cl}^-$ displacing iodine. Here we have ions and acids, not the displacement reaction, and it would go the opposite way.
options.B: Incorrect. Both $\text{HCl}$ and $\text{HI}$ are volatile gases. Volatility does not explain why sulfur is reduced to $\text{SO}_2$, $\text{S}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ only in the iodide case.
options.C: Correct. Iodide ions are larger and lose electrons more easily than chloride ions, so they are better reducing agents. They reduce concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ further to give $\text{I}_2$ plus $\text{SO}_2$, $\text{S}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{S}$, while chloride cannot.
options.D: Incorrect. The dehydrating action of concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is removal of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ from substances like carbohydrates or hydrated salts. Here sulfuric acid is acting as an oxidising agent, gaining electrons from $\text{I}^-$.
